about: Every fixture of this folder. A file under good/ must validate against 'schema'. A file under bad/ must be refused, and 'rule' says which rule it breaks; 'expect' names the schema keyword that refuses it and the place in the fixture where it does (a JSON Pointer, '' for the whole value). Files named c* were captured from the daemon by capture_today.py; files named h*, r* and b* were written by hand. Files named u-*, m-*, v-* and f-* were generated: each is a good fixture with one change (u: a field nobody defined added; m: a required field removed; v: a value replaced by one outside the list of allowed values; f: a fixed value replaced), and each proves the one rule its 'rule' names. 'of', on a good transcript line, names the event fixtures the line is the projection of: the first event of the log, then the line's own event.

fixtures.shows: A turn in progress. created_at is the time of the event that establishes the turn's creation: its first state.changed, seen as it was made (reason commit), in a log that is whole up to it. updated_at is the time of its latest state.changed. Both are times the core logged.
An approval is pending for the turn: a person must answer it on a surface that draws approvals. It is never answered through the Task.
The turn ended and its work is done. The result is the turn's own, and it expires when the turn's does.
The turn is over, so the Task is completed; its outcome says the engine waits for the user, which is not 'done'.
The turn failed with a typed code. The worker is gone.
Cancelling a turn's Task is an interrupt of that turn, not a Stop: the Task is cancelled because the turn's outcome is 'interrupted', and the worker lives on.
The run was stopped and the Stop was confirmed: the turn's Task is cancelled. 'cancelled' is never shown before that.
A Stop of the session was asked and is not confirmed: the turn is still working, with cancel_requested true.
A turn that waits behind the turn in progress: it is bound to no run yet, and its only event is the one that recorded it.
An earlier turn of a run that a later turn shares. Its Task carries its own result and its own times; nothing of the later turn, though that one ended last on the same run.

Work started with run.start and no session: the Task id is the run id, there is no session and no turn, and it does not expire. Its times are those of the run's own log, 'run:<run_id>'. That log begins with a snapshot: the run already existed when logging began, so nothing retained establishes when it was created, and created_at is null. A snapshot is not a creation. updated_at is the time of the latest state.changed all the same.
A run that is being started: working. Its log holds one event so far, a snapshot: updated_at is that event's time and created_at is null.
An approval is pending for the run.
A Stop was asked and is not confirmed. The Task keeps the status it had, working, and says cancel_requested. It is not 'cancelled'.
The Stop is confirmed: only now is the Task cancelled.
The run ended and its result says ok: completed. The Task carries the result's code and detail and names the run as where the whole result is read (run.status).
The run ended and its result is an error: failed, with the result's own code.
The run ended and there is no result to read: failed, with the code result_unavailable. It is never shown as completed.

A start that never launched, as the record is today: nothing durable says why, so the code is start_failed and the detail is null. The log holds nothing of it either, so both times are null. The Task invents none of this.
RESERVED: the same, once the record carries start_error (the lane that owns Stop writes it). The Task's detail is then that code.
The machine restarted under the run: failed, with the code lost_reboot.
The unit cannot be observed: nobody can say that the run ended, so the Task is still working.
A result that breaks the route contract's own rule: it says ok and carries a code. The Task goes by the code: failed, never completed.
The other way to break it: the result says error and names no code. The Task is failed, with the code result_invalid, and invents no reason.
A view whose state is stop_pending and whose stop record is null: the schema takes it, so the rule answers it. The state alone says a Stop was asked and is not confirmed.
The log as it is retained begins at position 4: the events before it were dropped. The first event that is left is not the turn's creation, so created_at is null. A tail is not a creation time.
The log begins at its first position, and a replay.gap stands before the first event of this turn: the turn's creation may be in the gap, so created_at is null.
A gap later in the log does not hide the origin: the run's first record is the commit that made it, nothing is missing before it, and created_at is its time.
A run made after logging began. Its first record is the commit that made it (reason commit, at position 1, nothing missing before it): that event establishes its creation, and created_at is its time.
A run whose first record was found by a later scan (reason reconcile): earlier steps may be missing, so it does not establish the creation either. created_at is null.
A turn whose first record is a snapshot: it already existed when logging began. Position 1 and no gap before it say that nothing was dropped, not that the turn was made then. created_at is null.

The first events filed under this turn are the engine's acceptance and the turn's start; its record is first logged after them, as it was made. The creation is that first record, not the first event that names the turn.
A gap that stands for one position: the numbers a reader sees have no hole, 1, 2, 3, and the event the gap stands for may have been this turn's first record. created_at is null.

fixtures.rule: A request names a method of the table.
run.stop takes a run id and nothing else: a Stop never needs a key or a revision.
Every mutating method except run.start and run.stop takes a command_id.
A turn names the revision it read, so a stale client cannot act on old state.
An answer names the digest that was drawn.
An answer is 'approve' or 'deny'.
A projection is 'raw' or 'transcript'.
The principal comes from the way the request came in, never from its params.
A run's owner is derived by the server, never taken from params.
An update names the text or the delivery to change.
A 'conflict' says which: a reused id, a stale revision or turn, or an answer that came first.
A method answers only the codes its row lists: run.status is never 'busy'.
A method that is not in the table is answered method_unknown, never something else.
'unsupported' says why: not_implemented, or the driver flag that is missing.
With projection 'transcript' the answer carries lines, not events.
A 'started' answer carries the run and whether it was a retry.
events.follow waits at most 30 seconds.
The row of run.stop can never require a key or a revision.
A mutating method other than run.start and run.stop is keyed by command_id.
A method that needs 'approve' is never offered as an MCP tool.
A method that changes nothing takes no key and no revision.
A row lists codes from the table's own list.
A refusal's code is a refusal.
An unconfirmed start names the run, by its view or by its id; it is never a bare code.
A failed start names the run id and says why; it is never a bare refusal.
The code of a start error is a plain word. What follows a colon belongs in the detail.
'start_unconfirmed' is run.start's own answer, never a refusal: no other method can give it.
A read takes the cursor a read returned: the log, the place in it and the epoch travel together, and a bare number beside it is refused.
A read names its place with a cursor; a log id alone is not one.
Every page says whether the daemon restarted since the cursor was given.
Only a method that takes a command_id needs a receipt: a read is never refused store_absent.
When an interrupt fell back to Stop, the answer carries the Stop's own answer: a pending Stop must reach the caller.
run.status waits on no service: its 'unavailable' is the closing daemon and nothing else.
'unavailable' says why.
run.start's 'unavailable' is the closing daemon or a start registrant that refused.
service_starting is the readiness of the service a row names. session.status's row names none, so it can never say it.
plugin.list names no service either: its 'unavailable' is the closing daemon or its own legacy refusal, no plugin host.
The interrupt fell back to Stop and the Stop is pending: the answer's code is pending. 'ok' would tell the caller the turn was dealt with.
The same Stop with a session that still says live: while a Stop is pending the session is stop_pending, and no resume is allowed until it is confirmed.
'pending' is the answer of a pending fallback Stop and of nothing else: an interrupt that was delivered is not pending.
A pending answer that carries a confirmed Stop contradicts itself.
Only an interrupt that fell back to Stop carries a Stop's answer.
